items.extracted_title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
items.extracted_excerpt: A Blog post by Ai2 on Hugging Face
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work. These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings. To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies. Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used. One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research. Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized. A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge. For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually. But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs. Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis. But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way. Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows. These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks. These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like. Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process? An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?” Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves. Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One

items.title_original: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
items.title_en: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
items.summary_zh: Hugging Face Blog 更新了实时语音交互模型能力，关键在于模型能力、部署成本、权限控制或开发者工作流的实际变化。

items.extracted_title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
items.extracted_excerpt: A Blog post by IBM Research on Hugging Face
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type. We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps. A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent: - Listens and turns the speech into text. - Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English. - Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says. - Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked. If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up. CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things: - One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting. - The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search(). - Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's. The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it. audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server. Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph. Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning. The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything. Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages. A few small decisions mattered more than we expected: - Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech. - Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC, and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast. - Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user. - Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key. You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer: Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn. Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent. Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust. This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity. If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core. New to CUGA? Here are some places to start: - cuga.dev: the CUGA home page. - CUGA on GitHub: the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue. - CUGA documentation: setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration. - CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub: the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space. Spaces you can try in your browser: - CUGA Agent: the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario. - CUGA Apps: launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard. - CUGA Policy Playground: two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without. More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog: - CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents: the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes. - Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness: the app gallery this voice agent belongs to. - Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA?: how much the harness matters when the model stays the same.

items.extracted_title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
items.extracted_excerpt: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here. One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py): - Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning. - Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs (control → candidate → control). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics. - Log every run in PLAN.md, including regressions and dead ends. - Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner. bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled. The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure: - HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver (jobs/driver.py) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang (lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini) and vLLM nightly (vllm/vllm-openai:nightly) in parallel. - CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields. - Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification. The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding. Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate. ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip. All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB: vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \ --tool-call-parser inkling \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser inkling \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work). Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits. Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer. Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower: We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup. items.title_original: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
items.title_en: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
items.summary_zh: DeepMind 的新访谈把焦点放在行业访谈中的判断与经验，适合观察 AI 产品负责人、创业者和研究者如何判断下一阶段应用边界。
items.summary_en: Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra.
items.extracted_title: Identifying Molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Antigravity â Google DeepMind
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model. Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into. These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases. To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. Yet even after a decade of expanding reference libraries, spectral searches annotate on average only about 5% of measured spectra, and 10% for human samples; the rest has been called the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry. Many of the molecules producing these unannotated signals are already listed in public chemical databases, but their spectra have not been recorded, so there is no reference spectrum to compare against. Elucidating them instead requires inferring the structure directly from the observed fragment ions. Analytical chemists have a well-tested, step-by-step workflow for narrowing down candidate structures from tandem (MS/MS) spectra: check spectral reference libraries, find the molecular formula and retrieve candidate structures from chemical databases, and then test every candidate against observed fragment peaks. The tools for each step exist and are openly available, but running the full workflow would take a domain expert a significant amount of time for every single spectrum. Because a single study can produce thousands of spectra, manual analysis cannot keep up, leaving most of these signals unannotated. Today, we are sharing Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity, a suite of domain skills that pair Gemini's chemical reasoning with the ability to run established mass spectrometry tools and query public chemical databases on the user's behalf to fulfil their request. Antigravity runs these skills, combines their results, and reasons about the chemistry, laying out the evidence for a chemist to review. For molecules that are already catalogued in a database, identification is much faster. For undiscovered molecules, the agent still helps: it narrows down the formula and the parts of the structure supported by the fragments to guide full structure elucidation. A language model cannot do this on its own, since matching fragments to a structure takes precise mass calculations, searches across databases of millions of compounds, and simulations of how bonds break. Pairing Geminiâs reasoning with dedicated chemistry tools brings those steps into one workflow.

items.title_original: Introducing Hurdle: Run agent evals on your API, skills, and docs
items.title_en: Introducing Hurdle: Run agent evals on your API, skills, and docs
items.summary_zh: Claude 更新了AI 代理工程与工具调用能力，关键在于模型能力、部署成本、权限控制或开发者工作流的实际变化。

items.extracted_title: Introducing Hurdle: Run agent evals on your API, skills, and docs
items.extracted_excerpt: Hurdle is an open-source npm library for agent evals. Run Claude Code and Codex against real tasks on your API, score each run with code checks, guards and an LLM judge, and see which models and conditions pass.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: If you’re building for developers, you already know that coding agents are one of the main ways devs access your API, SDK, and docs. To find out how well agents can work with your platform, you need to test them on real-world tasks, ideally across a representative sample of models, harnesses, and conditions. Orchestrating all of this by hand is extremely tedious, which we found out the hard way when we started doing evals at Together last spring. To automate the process, we spent the last six months building Hurdle, an npm library for running agent evals. Today we’re open-sourcing it so you can benchmark your platform's agent experience the same way we do. Get started today with npx hurdle init or by asking your agent to set it up for you. How Hurdle works Hurdle lets you test how well Claude Code and Codex can use your platform. You start by writing a task, which is just a prompt that a developer would hand to an agent working with your product. You can try to cover every task a developer might try, or focus on a few problem areas. Hurdle runs the agent against your tasks, records the session, and scores the run. Exactly how scoring works is up to you. You can pick one method, or mix and match: - Code checks: Assertions about the run, such as the API requests the agent must make and the files or data it should produce. - Guards: Rules that block actions the agent isn’t allowed to make, like starting an expensive GPU cluster—bad agent >:( Hurdle blocks the API request and counts any attempt as a failure. - Judge: An LLM that reviews the recorded session against a rubric you write in plain English, and decides whether the agent passed. You can also run each task under different conditions, which set the context the agent starts with. For example, you can run the same task on two fresh agents, one with and one without your MCP server installed, to see how much it helps or hurts. Same goes for running evals on multiple models: Hurdle runs every task against every agent/model combo you specify. Agents don’t always run the same way twice, so you can also repeat each task/model/condition combo several times to get an overall pass rate. Example task: Find the cheapest GPU cluster Here’s a real task we came up with during our own eval adventures: List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. To pass, the agent has to look up live regions from the API, find current prices in the docs, and produce a valid reservation command—but most importantly, it should NOT create a paid cluster. Here’s how we wrote the first three requirements as Hurdle checks: And here’s the guard that prevents the agent from starting a real cluster. Hurdle enforces the guard while the agent works, and runs the checks after the agent finishes: The eval suite To run a task, you add it to a suite, a small file that picks the tasks to run, the agents and conditions to run them with, and how many times to repeat each run. For the GPU cluster task, we’re using both a deterministic code check and an LLM judge, so we set the suite's verdict to hybrid and name a judge model: Run and view results npx hurdle run runs the suite. Adding --view opens the results viewer when the suite finishes: Hurdle runs each task for every agent and condition in the suite, as many times as repeats says. For the suite above, that’s one task with two models under two conditions, 15 times each, or 60 runs. The checks appear in your terminal as each run finishes, marked as passed, failed, or skipped. The viewer shows the suite’s headline numbers at the top: pass rate, average duration, and average cost per run. Below that, a grid breaks down the pass rate by task and condition, so you can see which combos are failing: Click into a run to see exactly what the agent did, including a full transcript, a list of the agent's tool calls and API requests, plus the result of every check and the judge's final assessment. Hurdle saves the results to .hurdle/ in your project directory, so you can reopen the viewer by running npx hurdle view. Local runs For quick tests on tasks you trust, you can run your evals locally, much as you would if you were prompting the agent yourself. Hurdle starts the claude or codex CLI on your machine in a temporary workspace, hands it the task's prompt and files, and records the session. Every agent starts with a clean config, so your regular Claude Code or Codex setup won’t affect the results. Local runs come with two caveats: First, Hurdle can’t see or block the agent’s API requests, so you can’t use guards or request checks. But more importantly, the agent runs as you, so it can read local files and use your real API keys. For anything complex or risky, you should always use a sandbox. Sandboxed runs For production evaluations, Hurdle uses the Together Sandbox API to spin up isolated environments where coding agents can execute code, install dependencies, and interact with APIs without accessing your local machine. Each run gets a fresh sandbox, so agents start from a clean environment rather than inheriting files or state from previous runs. Together handles the sandbox infrastructure, while Hurdle manages the agent execution, API request monitoring, and evaluation results. When you start a sandboxed run, Hurdle launches a local proxy called Guardian, then opens a single WebSocket to Together, which boots a fresh Together Sandbox for the run. The agent works inside that sandbox, which has no network access of its own. Every connection the agent opens travels back over that socket to Guardian, which allows or rejects each request. Your keys never enter the sandbox—the agent gets random stand-ins, and when it calls your API, Guardian swaps in the real key and forwards the request. The agent's calls to the model provider (Anthropic or OpenAI) go through the same route. This routing is what lets Hurdle check requests, enforce guards, and keep your keys safe: - API request checks: Every request passes through Guardian, so your checks can see exactly which calls the agent made. - Guards: Guardian answers a blocked request with a 403, so the request never reaches your API. - Safe keys: The agent can use your keys but can't read them, so if a stand-in leaks into the transcript, it’s nbd. By default, the sandbox doesn't limit which endpoints the agent can call. The agent can send any request to your API with your key, so give your evals a dedicated key with a low balance, and add a guard for anything dangerous. Try it yourself You'll need Node.js 22.18 or later and the Claude Code or Codex CLI installed. 1. Set up your project Create a project in a new directory: To use Codex instead of Claude, add --agent codex: init creates an evals/ directory with a starter suite and example task. 2. Add your API keys Next, create a .env.local file in my-evals and add your Anthropic API key.
